n: David’s sons born during his seven years in Hebron are listed by mother. This royal family line is the center of the chronicler’s hope for Israel.

f.g: Called Chileab in 2 Samuel 3:3; not the prophet Daniel.

n: Absalom and Adonijah are named—both later tried to seize David’s throne. Absalom’s mother was a foreign princess, a marriage that sealed an alliance with Geshur.
David’s fifth and sixth sons, about whom little else is known.

f.g: Only Eglah is called “his wife,” though all these women were David’s wives.

n: David ruled in Hebron seven and a half years, then thirty-three years in Jerusalem—about forty years in all (about 1010–970 BC).
Four sons were born to Bath-shua (Bathsheba) in Jerusalem, including Nathan and Solomon. Luke traces Jesus’ ancestry through Nathan; Matthew traces it through Solomon.

f.g: Bathsheba; her father Ammiel is called Eliam in 2 Samuel 11:3.

n: More sons born to David in Jerusalem by other wives.
Nogah and Nepheg, two names not found in the parallel list in 2 Samuel—perhaps sons who died young.

f.g: “Brightness”; found also in 1 Chronicles 14:6 but not in 2 Samuel 5.

n: The last of nine Jerusalem-born sons. The repeated names (Elishama, Eliphelet) may honor brothers who had died.

f.g: “God is deliverance”; appears twice in this list.

n: Besides these were sons of David’s concubines and his daughter Tamar, whose tragic story is told in 2 Samuel 13.
The royal line now runs from Solomon through the kings of Judah, father to son—an unbroken chain of David’s house, as God had promised.

f.g: Abijah, also called Abijam in 1 Kings 15:1.

n: The list continues through Joram, Ahaziah and Joash. Queen Athaliah’s usurpation between Ahaziah and Joash is passed over, since she was not of David’s line.
Next come Amaziah, Azariah (better known as Uzziah) and Jotham—kings of the eighth century BC in the days of Isaiah.
Ahaz the unfaithful, Hezekiah the reformer and Manasseh the idolater: three very different kings in three generations.
The line reaches Amon and then Josiah, Judah’s great reforming king.
Josiah’s four sons; three of them ruled Judah in its final years. Shallum is better known as Jehoahaz.

f.g: Jehoahaz, who ruled only three months (2 Kings 23:31; Jeremiah 22:11).
Otherwise unknown; he may have died young.

n: Jehoiakim’s son Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) was taken to Babylon in 597 BC. The Zedekiah named here may be a different man from King Zedekiah, Josiah’s son.
Even in exile David’s line continues. Jeconiah’s son Salathiel (Shealtiel) appears in the genealogies of Jesus.

f.g: May mean “captive,” describing Jeconiah rather than naming a son.

n: Jeconiah had more sons in Babylon. Babylonian ration records mention provisions for his sons, confirming they lived there.

f.g: Some scholars connect him with Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah in Ezra 1:8, though this is uncertain.

n: Zerubbabel, who led the first return from exile and rebuilt the temple, is a grandson of Jeconiah. Elsewhere he is called Shealtiel’s son—perhaps through adoption or levirate marriage.

f.g: A daughter included in the royal line, unusual in such lists.

n: Zerubbabel had five more sons, whose names express hope: “thought of,” “tent,” “the LORD blesses,” “the LORD is kind,” and “kindness returns.”

f.g: “Kindness (or covenant love) will return”—a hopeful name for a child born after exile.

n: The line continues past Zerubbabel through Hananiah and several related families. The text here is difficult and may list branches rather than a single line.
Through Shechaniah and Shemaiah comes Hattush, who returned to Jerusalem with Ezra.
The descendants of Neariah carry the royal line into the Persian period.

f.g: A later descendant named after the great king, not King Hezekiah himself.

n: The genealogy ends about eight generations after Jeconiah, reaching close to the chronicler’s own time. David’s line has survived exile, keeping alive the hope of the Messiah, the Son of David.

f.g: “Cloud”; some ancient Jewish interpreters linked this name with the Messiah coming on the clouds (Daniel 7:13).
